election._note: By law no later than 8 October 2028; Wikipedia 'Next Luxembourg general election'. Hagenbach-Bischoff reduced to largest-remainder PR — see docs/electoral-systems.md.

dissolution._note: The Grand Duke may dissolve the Chamber on the government's advice; no codified lockout. New elections must be held within three months. constituteproject.org, Luxembourg 1868 (rev. 2009) Constitution.

amendment._note: A revision needs two votes three months apart, each by simple majority, then a binding referendum -- unless the second vote itself carries by 3/4 of the Chamber, which waives the referendum. This game models that referendum-waiving bar as the entrenching number, at its real fraction rather than rounded to an existing tier. constituteproject.org, Luxembourg 1868 (rev. 2009) Constitution, Art. 114.
amendment._permits_system_change_note: The Grand Ducal succession is itself governed by ordinary constitutional revision (Art. 114), not entrenched against it.

formation._note: Coalition government appointed by the Grand Duke; requires the confidence of the Chambre des Deputes on a simple majority.

government._pretender_note: Whom data/laws/amendments.json's Restoration Act puts on the throne. Authored per nation because the law is generic and the dynasty is not; a monarchy points this at its own sitting monarch.

fiscal._note: General government, IMF/OECD estimates ~2023-2024, rounded. V1.2a starting policy, derived from France's anchor (see FRA.json): VAT 17% is Luxembourg's own statutory standard rate, the lowest in the EU (Tax Foundation, 'VAT Rates in Europe 2024'). Corporate 24.9% is the commonly cited combined rate (17% corporate income tax plus municipal business tax plus solidarity surtax) -- used directly rather than revenue-share-scaled from France, for the same reason as Switzerland's: Luxembourg's corporate tax revenue is inflated by holding-company profit booking relative to what a modest headline rate would suggest. Income is France's 20 scaled by Luxembourg's OECD Revenue Statistics personal-tax-to-GDP share against France's, hence 17. Spending is France's split scaled by general government expenditure of 46.8% of GDP against France's 57.3% (tradingeconomics.com / Wikipedia 'Economy of Luxembourg').
